cards.title: Connect a bonus to the product with a logical positioning bridge
cards.summary: An apparently unrelated bonus can strengthen a product offer when its genuine benefit creates a clear contrast with the product’s deeper advantage.
cards.use_when: Choosing a gift-with-purchase, bundle bonus, subscription sign-up item, or loyalty reward that is adjacent to—but not identical with—the merchandise.
steps: Define the core function of the proposed bonus and the core outcome of the product being sold. Look for an honest distinction such as immediate access versus in-depth guidance, convenience versus durability, or inspiration versus implementation.

Write the offer sequence in two moves: acknowledge the real strength of the bonus, then explain why the purchased product provides the more complete or lasting result. Do not pretend the bonus is inferior; use it to dramatize the product’s positioning.

Use thematic adjacency rather than arbitrary expense. The source’s Newsweek example paired a radio with news coverage: radio was positioned as the fastest way to hear news, while the publication provided news in depth. A Swiss bank account similarly reinforced an offshore-investing newsletter’s privacy theme.

For a merchant, a travel organizer might be a credible bonus for premium luggage because it reinforces organized travel; explain the organizer’s quick-access role and the luggage’s role in protecting and carrying the full trip’s gear.
caveats: The connection must be truthful and understandable without a long explanation.
A costly but random gift can distract from the product or attract customers interested only in the bonus.

cards.title: Reduce opt-in and checkout friction with minimal required fields
cards.summary: Provide appropriate response channels and require only information needed to complete the current ecommerce action, because each forced field adds friction.
cards.use_when: Designing an email capture form, product waitlist, account creation flow, customer-service contact form, or ecommerce checkout.
steps: Match response methods to the action. On a product page or campaign landing page, make the primary online action obvious, and expose relevant alternatives such as chat, email, phone, or a store address when customers may prefer reassurance before buying.
For a newsletter, waitlist, or lead capture form, request only the minimum necessary information—typically email, with name only if it will actually improve subsequent communication.

Audit every required field in checkout and account creation. Keep fields required only when payment, delivery, fraud prevention, tax, or fulfillment genuinely requires them; make all other fields optional and label required fields clearly.

Turn convenience into copy where applicable. The source’s direct-mail example emphasized that the response card was already addressed and postage-paid. Ecommerce equivalents include guest checkout, saved address data, prefilled discount codes, and clearly stated delivery options.
caveats: The source gives directional advice that mandatory fields reduce response, not a modern ecommerce conversion-rate benchmark.
A purchase transaction necessarily requires more data than an email opt-in; do not remove fields needed for lawful payment and fulfillment.

cards.title: Use explicit no-pressure language for genuinely low-commitment offers
cards.summary: For a free resource or trial, clearly state the real follow-up and obligation terms so shoppers do not assume a hidden sales commitment.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for an email sign-up incentive, product quiz result, back-in-stock alert, sample request, free guide, or trial where customers may fear unwanted contact.
steps: Map the actual follow-up sequence before writing copy: whether the customer will receive only automated email, may receive SMS after consent, may be contacted by support, or will face no proactive contact at all.

State the low-commitment condition plainly beside the form or call to action. If no sales calls occur, say so; if the customer is joining an email list, state that accurately rather than implying no future messages.
Use the word “free” when the resource truly has no charge. The source argues that “free” is not inherently unprofessional, even for sophisticated buyers.
Add a direct statement of what the customer is not committing to, such as no purchase required, no subscription required, or no obligation beyond the disclosed communications.
caveats: Never claim that no one will call or that there is no follow-up if the business actually uses those channels.
The source’s cited six-fold attendance lift from a free diary is a single example, not an ecommerce result forecast.

cards.title: Stack credible bonuses and prove their stated value
cards.summary: Multiple bonuses can make a bundle more compelling when each is useful, clearly valued, and available at the stated price outside the promotion.
cards.use_when: Building a product bundle, subscription acquisition offer, digital companion pack, or purchase-threshold promotion.
steps: Select two or more bonuses that reduce a real barrier to using the main product, extend its use, or reinforce the buyer’s desired outcome. The source reports that information-product buyers often respond well to multiple premiums; apply that idea to commerce only where the extras remain relevant.
For digital guides, printable tools, recipes, setup instructions, or accessories, present each item separately with a specific function rather than as an undifferentiated pile of “free extras.”
Assign a stated value only when it is credible. A strong method from the source is to sell the same report or digital item separately in the store at the displayed price, making the claim verifiable.

Show the bundle math: itemize the normal prices, then state the bundle or subscription price. The source cites Michael Bell’s view that combined premium value should exceed the subscription price; treat that as an offer-design hypothesis, not a universal requirement.
caveats: The source’s Amazon case—roughly a dozen reports and more than 900 orders in one day—is a case example, not a predicted outcome.
Artificial “values” that are never charged in practice weaken trust and can create pricing-policy issues.

cards.title: Use first-order and completion rewards to drive repeat purchase
cards.summary: A bonus can either lower the risk of a first order or reward customers for completing a defined replenishment or collection journey.
cards.use_when: Designing a subscription launch, replenishment program, collectible series, loyalty milestone, or first-purchase acquisition offer.
steps: Choose the behavior to reward: first order, a specified number of reorders, completion of a collection, or a subscription retention milestone.

For first purchase, offer a meaningful welcome premium that helps the customer use the primary product. The source cites Gevalia’s free coffeemaker with an initial order in a monthly gourmet-coffee subscription.

For continuity, set a visible completion reward. The source’s Franklin Mint example shipped one chess piece per month and gave a free chessboard after all 32 pieces were purchased. A merchant could adapt this as a free storage case, accessory, or limited product after a defined number of qualifying replenishment orders.

Make qualification, timing, cancellations, and fulfillment terms clear in the program rules. Track completion rate, reward cost, repeat-order margin, and customer-service contacts—not merely enrollment.
caveats: Completion rewards create a future inventory obligation; reserve or source the final reward before promoting it.
Long purchase paths may frustrate customers if the reward feels too distant or the qualification mechanics are unclear.

cards.title: Treat classic direct-response offer mechanics as test hypotheses
cards.summary: Older direct-marketing rules of thumb can suggest offer tests, but a store should evaluate them on contribution margin, repeat purchasing, and refunds rather than response alone.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing experiments on payment terms, subscription structure, bonuses, discounts, or deferred-payment options for an ecommerce offer.
steps: Use Benson’s reported rules as a hypothesis backlog rather than a forecast: premiums may outperform cash discounts; memberships may renew better than plain subscriptions; installment terms may improve response for higher-priced items; and offering longer versus shorter terms may increase gross dollars while reducing the number of subscriptions.

Translate only mechanisms that fit the store. For example, test a relevant gift-with-purchase against an equivalent cash discount, or test a replenishment membership against one-time subscription access.
Define success before launch: completed purchases, gross margin after premium and payment costs, cancellation rate, refund rate, repeat purchase, and customer lifetime value.
Segment results by new versus returning customers and by acquisition source. An offer that lifts first-order conversion but attracts discount-only buyers may be unprofitable downstream.
caveats: The source attributes these heuristics to Dick Benson’s 1992 book; they are not verified modern ecommerce benchmarks.
Sweepstakes, “bill me” terms, credit, and installment promotions can introduce legal, fraud, and buyer-quality issues. Verify current platform, payment-provider, and legal requirements before use.

cards.title: Test price with positioning, not as an isolated lower-is-better choice
cards.summary: A low price can signal insufficient quality to a professional or high-intent segment, so test price alongside the audience and value proposition it communicates.
cards.use_when: Repositioning a product for a premium customer segment, deciding whether to introduce a higher-priced version, or diagnosing stalled sales at a low price point.
steps: Identify the intended customer and the quality signal they expect. Ask whether the current price makes the product seem inaccessible, cheap, incomplete, or not serious enough for its promised use.

Test a price change together with positioning that explains the product’s appropriate customer and use case. The source’s software example changed focus to professionals and raised price from $79 to $129; sales increased after the segment shift, so the result should not be interpreted as price alone causing the lift.
For merchandise, pair a premium price with concrete evidence: materials, construction, warranty, compatibility, origin, service, or performance details that substantiate the positioning.

Measure conversion rate, revenue per visitor, gross margin, refund rate, support burden, and repeat purchase at each price. Keep the experiment’s product availability and traffic source comparable where possible.
caveats: The cited example is a repositioning case, not proof that doubling a price will increase sales.
Price is only one offer component; the source also identifies payment terms, premium, and guarantee as important variables to test.

cards.title: Frame fixed savings in dollars and variable savings in percentages
cards.summary: When every eligible shopper receives the same monetary saving, a dollar-off message may be more concrete than the equivalent percentage; test the framing on your own catalog.
cards.use_when: Writing sale banners, email subject lines, coupon messages, or product-page promotions with an equivalent dollar-off and percentage-off expression.
steps: Determine whether the saving is actually fixed. If all customers receive the same $50 reduction, create a dollar-off version such as “$50 off.”
When the saving varies with the product, model, or cart value, a percentage message may communicate the offer more accurately, such as “15% off selected items.”

Test equivalent versions against the same audience and time period. The source reports a test in which a $50-off coupon generated nearly three times the revenue of a 15%-off coupon with the same $50 value.
Use the form that puts the most concrete truthful number first, but ensure exclusions, minimum spends, and eligible SKU rules are equally visible in both treatments.
caveats: The nearly-three-times result came from one reported email test and is not a universal conversion benchmark.
Do not use a percentage headline that obscures the actual savings, or a dollar headline that applies only to a narrow subset without clear disclosure.

cards.title: Make a lump-sum price easier to evaluate with truthful per-use math
cards.summary: For products or subscriptions used over a known period, per-day or per-use framing can contextualize the price without hiding the actual amount due.
cards.use_when: Merchandising annual subscriptions, replenishment plans, durable goods, multi-month supply bundles, or higher-ticket products on a PDP or landing page.
steps: Calculate the smaller unit using the real period of service or planned use. The source’s examples turn a $297 annual subscription into 81 cents per day and a $197 annual subscription into 54 cents per day.
Place the per-day figure near—not instead of—the full price and payment schedule. Customers must be able to see what they pay today and whether renewal is automatic.
Use this framing where the unit is meaningful: a 90-day skincare supply, annual membership, or product designed for daily use. Explain the usage assumption if it depends on a prescribed routine.

Avoid comparisons that make specialized products look artificially expensive, such as price per page versus mass-market books. Instead, tie the math to the actual duration or number of uses delivered.
caveats: Per-day math is a framing device, not a payment-term change.
Do not imply a guaranteed duration when individual use, consumption, or product lifespan varies materially.

cards.title: Anchor price against real alternatives that solve the same customer problem
cards.summary: Price becomes easier to accept when shoppers first see the credible cost, effort, or risk of alternative ways to achieve the same outcome.
cards.use_when: Writing a PDP, bundle page, comparison table, or acquisition landing page for a product whose price needs context.
steps: Identify the customer’s underlying job and the realistic alternatives: buying multiple separate items, paying for a service, replacing inferior products repeatedly, renting, traveling, or spending time assembling a solution.

State the alternative cost or burden before presenting your price. The source’s examples compare an exercise machine with the cost of gym membership and an investment newsletter with what private clients pay for similar advice.

Use only substantiated comparisons. For a merchant, a home-organization kit could be compared with purchasing its components separately or hiring an organizer only if the claimed prices and scope are accurate.

Explain meaningful differences in outcome. The comparison should not merely say another category costs more; it should show how the product addresses the same need with a different mix of convenience, ownership, time, or expertise.
caveats: The source allows cross-category comparisons, but they still must be fair and defensible.
Do not invent competitor pricing, professional-service fees, or savings claims; unsupported anchors damage credibility.

cards.title: Test installment and trial offers on collected revenue, not first-payment conversion
cards.summary: A lower initial payment or trial can reduce entry friction, but it must be evaluated against cancellations, payment failures, returns, and total cash collected.
cards.use_when: Setting payment options for a high-ticket product, prepaid replenishment plan, subscription, or a product that requires a paid trial before a customer can assess fit.
steps: Test a clear pay-in-full offer against a clearly disclosed installment option. The source cites a direct-response test where four quarterly payments of $39 outperformed $49 paid annually despite the installment plan costing more overall; this illustrates first-payment psychology, not a recommended price level.

If using a low-cost trial, make billing date, recurring amount, cancellation path, eligibility, and refund conditions prominent before card submission. The source describes a $1, 14-day trial designed to obtain card details for a monthly options course.
For products requiring time to assess, time upsells after the customer has had a chance to experience value rather than immediately stacking more commitments at checkout.
Measure authorization rate, first renewal, all successful payments, chargebacks, refund requests, support contacts, and net contribution margin by offer—not just initial orders.
caveats: Payment plans and negative-option trials are regulated and payment-provider-sensitive. Verify current legal and platform requirements before implementation.
Small entry payments can attract customers likely to cancel or fail future payments; do not treat a first-payment lift as profit.

cards.title: Use good-better-best bundles to give shoppers a clear value ladder
cards.summary: Three well-differentiated purchase options can raise order value by making the middle or best-value bundle easier to choose without removing a basic entry option.
cards.use_when: Creating product bundles, multi-packs, replenishment quantities, subscription plan tiers, or a pricing table for a core product line.
steps: Create three understandable choices around a real customer need: a single-unit or starter option, a sufficient multi-unit option, and a larger supply or complete kit with the strongest unit economics.
Differentiate tiers with genuine utility—quantity, complementary accessories, shipping treatment, convenience, or service—not arbitrary feature removal that makes the basic product unusable.

Use the source’s physical-product pattern where appropriate: the largest supply may include free shipping and useful premiums, the middle quantity may include one bonus and shipping, and the single unit may have no premium and standard shipping.

Label the economic logic plainly, such as “best value per use” or “most popular,” only when the calculation or observed sales supports it. Monitor whether the middle option is adequately useful and whether the best option remains profitable after gifts and freight.
caveats: The source says the middle option often wins, but supplies no measured split; customer preferences may favor entry or premium tiers instead.
Do not make a tier intentionally misleading or hide recurring-commitment differences between options.

cards.title: Design guarantees through four operational decisions
cards.summary: A guarantee needs clear choices about duration, conditions, covered costs, and refund activation so it lowers purchase risk without creating avoidable ambiguity.
cards.use_when: Creating or revising a return guarantee for physical goods, consumables, durable products, or digital products on a PDP and in store policies.
steps: Set the duration based on when a buyer can reasonably evaluate the product. The source notes 30 days is common and prefers 60 or 90 days for many direct-response offers, while warning that dated information products should not receive long windows. For merchandise, match the period to delivery, setup, and normal use.

Decide whether the guarantee is unconditional. The source argues that vague conditions such as “sincere effort” or “saleable condition” suppress response because customers expect a dispute. If conditions are necessary for hygiene, customization, safety, or abuse prevention, state them simply and specifically.
Define coverage: item price only, original shipping, return shipping, taxes, gifts, or bundles. Use “product refund” rather than “full refund” if shipping is excluded.
Explain activation: when the clock begins, where to initiate a return, whether used items qualify, what to send back, and when the refund is issued.
caveats: Guarantee and return policies must comply with applicable consumer law and payment-platform rules; obtain current legal review.
The source’s examples of double-money-back guarantees lifting attendance are case examples, not a recommendation or expected multiplier for products.

cards.title: Make the guarantee visible and simple at the purchase decision
cards.summary: A guarantee only reduces purchase anxiety if shoppers can notice, understand, and trust it before adding the product to cart.
cards.use_when: Laying out a product page, bundle page, cart drawer, checkout reassurance area, or promotional email for a product with a meaningful return policy.
steps: Give the guarantee a distinct, descriptive heading such as “60-Day Try-It-At-Home Guarantee” or “Easy Returns,” rather than burying it in general terms and conditions.

Place the core promise near the price or add-to-cart action, then link to the full policy. Use a bordered card, certificate-style module, or other visible treatment; the source recommends large bold heading text and avoiding tiny footnote treatment.
State the buyer-facing outcome in plain language: what qualifies, the deadline, how to start, what amount is refunded, and whether original or return shipping is included.

Make the visible claim match operations exactly. If a used consumable can be returned, say so; if personalized merchandise cannot be returned except for defects, do not use an unconditional visual promise.
caveats: Prominence cannot compensate for conditional or confusing terms; it may increase distrust if the linked policy contradicts the headline.
Visual presentation should support accessibility and remain readable on mobile devices.

cards.title: Consider keep-the-download refunds for low-abuse digital products
cards.summary: For non-returnable digital goods, openly allowing a refund while the buyer keeps the file can reduce perceived risk, provided the merchant monitors abuse and economics.
cards.use_when: Selling ebooks, templates, printables, downloadable guides, digital patterns, or similar files that cannot practically be recovered after delivery.
steps: Recognize the operational reality: buyers can retain a downloaded file even if a policy demands deletion. Decide whether a trust-forward refund promise is preferable to an unenforceable restriction.

Test a clear guarantee that says the buyer may request a refund within the stated window and keep the file. The source reports that its own ebook refunds were a tiny fraction of one percent and cites David Powers reporting a 21% conversion and sales increase after adopting such language.

Set a limited, clearly stated refund window and publish the request process. Track conversion, refund rate, repeat customer rate, chargebacks, and unusually repetitive claims by customer or acquisition source.

Apply the policy selectively where the product is relatively low-cost, where goodwill matters, and where the expected abuse cost is tolerable. Keep fraud controls and support escalation procedures separate from ordinary refund requests.
caveats: The reported 21% lift is one marketer’s result, not an expected outcome.
This approach is not suitable for every digital asset, particularly high-value software, licenses, credentials, or files likely to be redistributed at scale.

cards.title: Use real deadlines and credible inventory scarcity
cards.summary: Urgency works when a sale end date or stock limit is operationally true, communicated consistently, and actually enforced.
cards.use_when: Planning a seasonal promotion, product drop, limited-edition launch, preorder, email campaign, cart promotion, or low-stock PDP message.
steps: Choose the appropriate constraint: a genuine promotion end date, a response window, a limited quantity, capacity for a handmade or customized run, or an event-like enrollment limit.

Use a specific calendar deadline only when campaign timing is fully controlled. The source distinguishes this from generic response windows used in direct mail; in ecommerce, a live date and time is usually preferable when the storefront and emails can be updated reliably.

Give a truthful reason for scarcity when one exists: manufacturing capacity, limited-edition production, remaining stock, preorder allocation, personalization slots, or event seats. The source stresses that a downloadable file cannot credibly be described as limited to a fixed number of copies.
Use reminder communication near a real expiry and stop the offer when promised. Confirm inventory synchronization across storefront, ads, email, and customer support before launch.
caveats: Do not reset or extend supposedly final deadlines without an honest explanation; repeated false urgency trains customers to wait.
The source advises legal review for time-limited promotional copy. Verify current consumer-protection and advertising requirements in relevant markets.

cards.title: Select purchase bonuses differently from lead-capture incentives
cards.summary: For a purchase offer, desirability can be the main bonus criterion; for email acquisition, relevance often matters more because unrelated gifts can attract low-intent freebie seekers.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a gift-with-purchase, an email sign-up incentive, a B2B sample offer, or a corporate buying promotion.
steps: Separate the business objective before selecting the premium. For an immediate sale, assess whether the gift raises perceived value enough to improve profitable conversion. Dick Benson’s view in the source is that relevance is secondary to desirability for sales premiums.

For lead capture, prioritize a resource or incentive related to the products the subscriber may later buy. The source disagrees with Benson in this context because unrelated high-value gifts can produce freebie seekers rather than qualified future customers.

For a consumer store, test relevant incentives such as a care guide, sizing guide, recipe pack, compatibility checklist, sample, or accessory against a broader gift, then compare downstream first purchase—not sign-ups alone.

For business buyers, avoid personal gifts that can trigger procurement or ethics concerns. The source cites a test where a discount plus clock radio performed worse than the same discount alone; a company-useful item may be safer if permitted.
caveats: The B2B gift result is context-specific and should not be generalized to consumer commerce.
Ensure gifts, sampling, and incentive practices comply with platform, employer, tax, and local promotional rules.

The source reports a test in which a $50-off coupon generated nearly three times the revenue of a 15%-off coupon with the same $50 value.","Use the form that puts the most concrete truthful number first, but ensure exclusions, minimum spends, and eligible SKU rules are equally visible in both treatments."],"caveats":["The nearly-three-times result came from one reported email test and is not a universal conversion benchmark.","Do not use a percentage headline that obscures the actual savings, or a dollar headline that applies only to a narrow subset without clear disclosure."],"tags":["offers","pricing","copywriting","email-marketing","promotion-design","experiment-design"]},{"title":"Make a lump-sum price easier to evaluate with truthful per-use math","summary":"For products or subscriptions used over a known period, per-day or per-use framing can contextualize the price without hiding the actual amount due.","use_when":"Merchandising annual subscriptions, replenishment plans, durable goods, multi-month supply bundles, or higher-ticket products on a PDP or landing page.","steps":["Calculate the smaller unit using the real period of service or planned use. The source’s examples turn a $297 annual subscription into 81 cents per day and a $197 annual subscription into 54 cents per day.","Place the per-day figure near—not instead of—the full price and payment schedule. Customers must be able to see what they pay today and whether renewal is automatic.","Use this framing where the unit is meaningful: a 90-day skincare supply, annual membership, or product designed for daily use. Explain the usage assumption if it depends on a prescribed routine.","Avoid comparisons that make specialized products look artificially expensive, such as price per page versus mass-market books. Instead, tie the math to the actual duration or number of uses delivered."],"caveats":["Per-day math is a framing device, not a payment-term change.","Do not imply a guaranteed duration when individual use, consumption, or product lifespan varies materially."],"tags":["offers","pricing","value-framing","subscriptions","product-page","copywriting"]},{"title":"Anchor price against real alternatives that solve the same customer problem","summary":"Price becomes easier to accept when shoppers first see the credible cost, effort, or risk of alternative ways to achieve the same outcome.","use_when":"Writing a PDP, bundle page, comparison table, or acquisition landing page for a product whose price needs context.","steps":["Identify the customer’s underlying job and the realistic alternatives: buying multiple separate items, paying for a service, replacing inferior products repeatedly, renting, traveling, or spending time assembling a solution.","State the alternative cost or burden before presenting your price. The source’s examples compare an exercise machine with the cost of gym membership and an investment newsletter with what private clients pay for similar advice.","Use only substantiated comparisons. For a merchant, a home-organization kit could be compared with purchasing its components separately or hiring an organizer only if the claimed prices and scope are accurate.","Explain meaningful differences in outcome. The comparison should not merely say another category costs more; it should show how the product addresses the same need with a different mix of convenience, ownership, time, or expertise."],"caveats":["The source allows cross-category comparisons, but they still must be fair and defensible.","Do not invent competitor pricing, professional-service fees, or savings claims; unsupported anchors damage credibility."],"tags":["offers","pricing","positioning","value-framing","product-page","copywriting"]},{"title":"Test installment and trial offers on collected revenue, not first-payment conversion","summary":"A lower initial payment or trial can reduce entry friction, but it must be evaluated against cancellations, payment failures, returns, and total cash collected.","use_when":"Setting payment options for a high-ticket product, prepaid replenishment plan, subscription, or a product that requires a paid trial before a customer can assess fit.","steps":["Test a clear pay-in-full offer against a clearly disclosed installment option. The source cites a direct-response test where four quarterly payments of $39 outperformed $49 paid annually despite the installment plan costing more overall; this illustrates first-payment psychology, not a recommended price level.","If using a low-cost trial, make billing date, recurring amount, cancellation path, eligibility, and refund conditions prominent before card submission. The source describes a $1, 14-day trial designed to obtain card details for a monthly options course.","For products requiring time to assess, time upsells after the customer has had a chance to experience value rather than immediately stacking more commitments at checkout.","Measure authorization rate, first renewal, all successful payments, chargebacks, refund requests, support contacts, and net contribution margin by offer—not just initial orders."],"caveats":["Payment plans and negative-option trials are regulated and payment-provider-sensitive. Verify current legal and platform requirements before implementation.","Small entry payments can attract customers likely to cancel or fail future payments; do not treat a first-payment lift as profit."],"tags":["offers","pricing","payment-terms","subscriptions","trial-offers","measurement"]},{"title":"Use good-better-best bundles to give shoppers a clear value ladder","summary":"Three well-differentiated purchase options can raise order value by making the middle or best-value bundle easier to choose without removing a basic entry option.","use_when":"Creating product bundles, multi-packs, replenishment quantities, subscription plan tiers, or a pricing table for a core product line.","steps":["Create three understandable choices around a real customer need: a single-unit or starter option, a sufficient multi-unit option, and a larger supply or complete kit with the strongest unit economics.","Differentiate tiers with genuine utility—quantity, complementary accessories, shipping treatment, convenience, or service—not arbitrary feature removal that makes the basic product unusable.","Use the source’s physical-product pattern where appropriate: the largest supply may include free shipping and useful premiums, the middle quantity may include one bonus and shipping, and the single unit may have no premium and standard shipping.","Label the economic logic plainly, such as “best value per use” or “most popular,” only when the calculation or observed sales supports it. Monitor whether the middle option is adequately useful and whether the best option remains profitable after gifts and freight."],"caveats":["The source says the middle option often wins, but supplies no measured split; customer preferences may favor entry or premium tiers instead.","Do not make a tier intentionally misleading or hide recurring-commitment differences between options."],"tags":["offers","pricing","offer-design","bundles","average-order-value","merchandising"]},{"title":"Design guarantees through four operational decisions","summary":"A guarantee needs clear choices about duration, conditions, covered costs, and refund activation so it lowers purchase risk without creating avoidable ambiguity.","use_when":"Creating or revising a return guarantee for physical goods, consumables, durable products, or digital products on a PDP and in store policies.","steps":["Set the duration based on when a buyer can reasonably evaluate the product. The source notes 30 days is common and prefers 60 or 90 days for many direct-response offers, while warning that dated information products should not receive long windows. For merchandise, match the period to delivery, setup, and normal use.","Decide whether the guarantee is unconditional. The source argues that vague conditions such as “sincere effort” or “saleable condition” suppress response because customers expect a dispute. If conditions are necessary for hygiene, customization, safety, or abuse prevention, state them simply and specifically.","Define coverage: item price only, original shipping, return shipping, taxes, gifts, or bundles. Use “product refund” rather than “full refund” if shipping is excluded.","Explain activation: when the clock begins, where to initiate a return, whether used items qualify, what to send back, and when the refund is issued."],"caveats":["Guarantee and return policies must comply with applicable consumer law and payment-platform rules; obtain current legal review.","The source’s examples of double-money-back guarantees lifting attendance are case examples, not a recommendation or expected multiplier for products."],"tags":["offers","risk-reversal","guarantees","returns-policy","product-page","customer-experience"]},{"title":"Make the guarantee visible and simple at the purchase decision","summary":"A guarantee only reduces purchase anxiety if shoppers can notice, understand, and trust it before adding the product to cart.","use_when":"Laying out a product page, bundle page, cart drawer, checkout reassurance area, or promotional email for a product with a meaningful return policy.","steps":["Give the guarantee a distinct, descriptive heading such as “60-Day Try-It-At-Home Guarantee” or “Easy Returns,” rather than burying it in general terms and conditions.","Place the core promise near the price or add-to-cart action, then link to the full policy. Use a bordered card, certificate-style module, or other visible treatment; the source recommends large bold heading text and avoiding tiny footnote treatment.","State the buyer-facing outcome in plain language: what qualifies, the deadline, how to start, what amount is refunded, and whether original or return shipping is included.","Make the visible claim match operations exactly. If a used consumable can be returned, say so; if personalized merchandise cannot be returned except for defects, do not use an unconditional visual promise."],"caveats":["Prominence cannot compensate for conditional or confusing terms; it may increase distrust if the linked policy contradicts the headline.","Visual presentation should support accessibility and remain readable on mobile devices."],"tags":["offers","risk-reversal","guarantees","product-page","checkout","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Consider keep-the-download refunds for low-abuse digital products","summary":"For non-returnable digital goods, openly allowing a refund while the buyer keeps the file can reduce perceived risk, provided the merchant monitors abuse and economics.","use_when":"Selling ebooks, templates, printables, downloadable guides, digital patterns, or similar files that cannot practically be recovered after delivery.","steps":["Recognize the operational reality: buyers can retain a downloaded file even if a policy demands deletion. Decide whether a trust-forward refund promise is preferable to an unenforceable restriction.","Test a clear guarantee that says the buyer may request a refund within the stated window and keep the file. The source reports that its own ebook refunds were a tiny fraction of one percent and cites David Powers reporting a 21% conversion and sales increase after adopting such language.","Set a limited, clearly stated refund window and publish the request process. Track conversion, refund rate, repeat customer rate, chargebacks, and unusually repetitive claims by customer or acquisition source.","Apply the policy selectively where the product is relatively low-cost, where goodwill matters, and where the expected abuse cost is tolerable. Keep fraud controls and support escalation procedures separate from ordinary refund requests."],"caveats":["The reported 21% lift is one marketer’s result, not an expected outcome.","This approach is not suitable for every digital asset, particularly high-value software, licenses, credentials, or files likely to be redistributed at scale."],"tags":["offers","risk-reversal","guarantees","digital-products","conversion-optimization","returns-policy"]},{"title":"Use real deadlines and credible inventory scarcity","summary":"Urgency works when a sale end date or stock limit is operationally true, communicated consistently, and actually enforced.","use_when":"Planning a seasonal promotion, product drop, limited-edition launch, preorder, email campaign, cart promotion, or low-stock PDP message.","steps":["Choose the appropriate constraint: a genuine promotion end date, a response window, a limited quantity, capacity for a handmade or customized run, or an event-like enrollment limit.","Use a specific calendar deadline only when campaign timing is fully controlled. The source distinguishes this from generic response windows used in direct mail; in ecommerce, a live date and time is usually preferable when the storefront and emails can be updated reliably.","Give a truthful reason for scarcity when one exists: manufacturing capacity, limited-edition production, remaining stock, preorder allocation, personalization slots, or event seats. The source stresses that a downloadable file cannot credibly be described as limited to a fixed number of copies.","Use reminder communication near a real expiry and stop the offer when promised. Confirm inventory synchronization across storefront, ads, email, and customer support before launch."],"caveats":["Do not reset or extend supposedly final deadlines without an honest explanation; repeated false urgency trains customers to wait.","The source advises legal review for time-limited promotional copy. Verify current consumer-protection and advertising requirements in relevant markets."],"tags":["offers","urgency","scarcity","promotion-design","email-marketing","landing-page"]},{"title":"Select purchase bonuses differently from lead-capture incentives","summary":"For a purchase offer, desirability can be the main bonus criterion; for email acquisition, relevance often matters more because unrelated gifts can attract low-intent freebie seekers.","use_when":"Choosing between a gift-with-purchase, an email sign-up incentive, a B2B sample offer, or a corporate buying promotion.","steps":["Separate the business objective before selecting the premium. For an immediate sale, assess whether the gift raises perceived value enough to improve profitable conversion. input.source_name: How to Create Irresistible Offers The Easiest Way on Earth to Make Your Marketing Generate More Leads, Orders, and Sales (1).docx

cards.title: Connect unrelated premiums to your product with a logical bridge
cards.summary: Even a premium that seems unrelated to your product can work if the copy connects it to the product's USP through a logical comparison.
cards.use_when: Choosing a premium or bonus item for a subscription box, membership, bundle or information product where the obvious physical premium seems off-category.
steps: Identify the premium's core function and the product's core function, then find the distinction that makes the product superior (speed vs. depth, headline vs. detail, summary vs. analysis).
Write copy that first credits the premium with its genuine strength, then pivots to why the product is the better or more complete resource.
Example from the source: Newsweek offered a free AM/FM radio. Milt Pierce's letter said the radio is the fastest way to get the news, but Newsweek is the best way to get news in depth.
For a Swiss-bank-account-branded investment newsletter, a free Swiss bank account premium dramatized the USP of offshore investing and privacy.
caveats: The bridge must be honest: the premium's strength is stated first, not dismissed.
This works best when the premium is thematically adjacent to the buyer's aspiration, not merely expensive.

cards.title: Reduce friction to accept: multiple response channels and minimal form fields
cards.summary: Offer every plausible way to respond and ask for the fewest fields possible, because each forced field incrementally reduces conversion.
cards.use_when: Designing order forms, lead capture pages, opt-in flows or checkout forms on an ecommerce site.
steps: Offer multiple response mechanisms: toll-free phone, chat, landing page link, email and postal address. Different prospects respond different ways.
On the web, ask for the minimum: for opt-in list building, name and email only.
When multiple fields exist, mark mandatory fields with an asterisk and make as many fields optional as possible. Conversion declines with each additional required field.
Turn the reply mechanism into a stated benefit where possible. Sig Rosenblum's Board Report letter said the card was already addressed and postage was paid.
caveats: The source states conversion declines incrementally per forced field but gives no specific numeric rate for ecommerce checkout; treat it as direction, not a benchmark.
Payment-required purchases will inherently need more fields than pure lead capture.

cards.title: Remove risk and obligation to lower sales pressure
cards.summary: Explicitly state that the prospect faces no sales visit, no call and no obligation, and use the word 'free' rather than 'complimentary'.
cards.use_when: Writing offer copy for lead magnets, whitepapers, webinars, trials or any offer where prospects fear being pursued by sales after signing up.
steps: If leads are followed up by phone rather than field sales, say 'No salesperson will visit' in the copy.
If leads are not followed up by phone, say 'No salesperson will call.'

When something is free, call it free. Do not substitute 'complimentary' for a high-level business audience out of fear 'free' sounds unprofessional — the source argues it does not offend and everyone wants free things.
State that no further action is required after acceptance: 'There's no obligation … nothing to buy … and no commitment of any kind.'
caveats: The A/B test cited (a free pocket diary lifting doctor symposium attendance six-fold) is a single example, not a guaranteed multiplier for ecommerce.
Only claim 'no salesperson will call' if that is operationally true; false claims create support and trust problems.

cards.title: Use multiple premiums and value them credibly
cards.summary: Two premiums are often better than one, especially for information buyers, and assigning a real, demonstrable dollar value to each premium increases believability.
cards.use_when: Building a stacked offer or bundle for a subscription, course, book or product where bonus items are included.
steps: Consider offering two or more premiums; Dick Benson's Secrets of Successful Direct Mail states two premiums are frequently better than one, and information-product buyers especially like multiple premiums.

For digital premiums (PDFs, downloadable reports, bonus guides), delivery cost is near zero, so the number can be large. The source cites a book promotion with roughly a dozen free special reports that reached #1 nonfiction on Amazon with 900+ orders in a day.
Assign a dollar value by printing a price in the upper right corner of the report cover.
Prove the price is real by selling the same reports in a cart on your main site at that price; then you can honestly say 'we actually sell this report at this price on our website.'
Michael Bell of Phillips Publishing suggests the combined stated value of the premiums should exceed the subscription price so the buyer gets their money's worth from premiums alone.
caveats: The Amazon result is a case example, not a promised outcome.
Inflated valuations without a real cart price undermine the credibility the technique depends on.

cards.title: Premiums as first-purchase and continuity incentives
cards.summary: Premiums can be structured to trigger first purchase or to keep customers buying through a series.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription boxes, continuity programs, collectible series or first-order incentives for an online store.
steps: Use a first-order premium to convert new customers. Gevalia offered a free 12-cup coffeemaker with the first order of a monthly gourmet coffee subscription.
Use a completion premium to drive series collection. Franklin Mint's Civil War chess set shipped one piece per month; after all 32 pieces were purchased, the customer received a free chessboard.
For ecommerce, the equivalent is a bonus item unlocked at a purchase threshold or after a set number of reorders.
caveats: Completion premiums create a long commitment and require inventory planning for the eventual free item.
The source presents these as examples of incentive design, not tested uplift figures.

cards.title: Benson's rules of thumb for offer mechanics
cards.summary: A set of direct-marketing rules of thumb from Dick Benson covering sweepstakes, bill-me terms, memberships, installments and premium-versus-discount choices.
cards.use_when: Choosing which offer mechanism to test first, or sizing the expected direction of an offer test on payment terms or premium structure.
steps: These are the source's reported rules of thumb from Benson's Secrets of Successful Direct Mail:
Sweepstakes improve results by 50 percent or more.
A credit or bill-me offer improves results by 50 percent or more.
Memberships renew better than plain subscriptions by 10 percent or more.
Adding installment payments for items over $15 increases results by 15 percent.
If you must choose one, premiums work better than cash discounts.
Subscriptions sold at half price for at least eight months convert at renewal just as strongly as full-price annual subscriptions.
Offering a choice of terms (one year vs. two years) pulls more gross dollars but about 10 percent fewer subscriptions.
Offering an incentive to pay cash when both cash and credit are offered reduces net response.
caveats: These are general direct-marketing heuristics from a 1992 book, not verified benchmarks for modern ecommerce. Treat them as test hypotheses.
Sweepstakes and bill-me terms may attract lower-quality buyers; measure downstream value, not just response.

cards.title: Price can be raised to increase sales when the price signals quality
cards.summary: A price that is too low for a professional audience can signal 'not a serious tool', while doubling the price can increase sales with that audience.
cards.use_when: Repositioning a product toward a professional or higher-intent customer segment, or when low-price positioning has stalled.
steps: Recognize that pricing is often counterintuitive: the price you assume sells best frequently does not.
Example from the source: a software company priced at $79 per desktop to appeal to both consumers and professionals; consumers found it too high and professionals read it as not serious.
They refocused on the professional market and raised the price to $129. Sales soared.
Test price points as part of the offer rather than assuming lower is always better.
caveats: This result came from a deliberate segment shift, not a pure price test on the same audience. Raising price without changing positioning or audience may not reproduce it.
The source names price as probably the most important component to test, alongside payment terms, premium and guarantee.

cards.title: State discounts as dollar amounts, not percentages, when the value is fixed
cards.summary: When a discount has a fixed dollar value, lead with the dollar figure, which generated nearly three times the revenue of the equivalent percentage in an email test.
cards.use_when: Writing coupon, sale or email subject-line copy where the savings amount is the same regardless of format.
steps: Test '$50-off coupon' against '15%-off coupon' where both equal a $50 discount. The source reports the $50-off version generated nearly three times more revenue.

Use percentage framing where the discount is inherently a fixed percentage and the dollar value varies by product, model or option selected. Geico's '15 minutes could save you 15 percent' is the cited percentage example.
Choose the framing that puts the more concrete number in front of the buyer.
caveats: The nearly-3x result is from one cited test reported in The Marketing Report (9/8/08); treat as a hypothesis to test on your own list.
Both framings can work; the rule is about which number is fixed and which is variable.

cards.title: Make an expensive price feel smaller: per-day math
cards.summary: Divide the total price by the days or period of use to state a much smaller daily figure in the copy.
cards.use_when: Selling annual subscriptions, memberships or high-ticket items where the lump sum causes resistance on the product page or sales email.
steps: Divide the total price by the length of service. Example: Georgia Publishing's American Speaker at $297 for a year's subscription becomes 'just 81 cents a day.'
An options trading course at $29.95/month can be stated as 'less than a dollar a day.'
An annual subscription at $197 becomes '54 cents a day.'

Warning from the source: divide by length of service or subscription, but avoid price-per-book or price-per-page comparisons, because specialized information always looks expensive per page next to trade books and periodicals.
caveats: This is a framing device, not a change to actual payment terms. If the buyer must pay the full sum up front, the copy should still be clear about that.

cards.title: Compare price against other categories addressing the same need
cards.summary: Anchor your price against more expensive alternatives in other categories that satisfy the same underlying need.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy for products with higher-priced substitutes or do-it-yourself alternatives (ecommerce physical goods, courses, tools, services).
steps: Identify what the buyer would otherwise spend to solve the same problem, including services a professional would charge for.

The source's examples: an ab machine compared to 'thousands on an expensive gym membership', priced at three payments of $19.95; a newsletter with the same stock recommendations that private clients pay $2,000 a year for.
Talk about the higher-priced options and alternatives first, so the actual price lands as a relief.
Cialdini's retail example: placing even more expensive sweaters at the store entrance made the intended line feel like a bargain by the time customers reached it.
caveats: Comparisons must be defensible; the source explicitly endorses apples-to-oranges comparisons against consultation or training, but the comparison still has to be honest to hold up.
Do not invent competitor prices or service costs.

cards.title: Exploit the first-payment effect with installments and low-entry trials
cards.summary: Buyers psychologically react to the first payment and discount future payments, so a higher total split into installments can outsell a lower lump sum.
cards.use_when: Setting payment terms for courses, subscriptions, software and higher-priced products in an ecommerce checkout.
steps: Design offers so the first payment is the small, decision-relevant number.
A/B test cited: $49 for one year vs. four quarterly payments of $39 (= $156/year). The $156 offer won, more than tripling the stated cost, because prospects mentally compared $49 to $39.

A $1 14-day trial can be used to capture card details: the source describes an options course at $29.95/month that added a $1 14-day trial with cancellation and refund available, which significantly increased sales. The $1 existed to get the card submitted, not to process revenue.
Rodale's book offers, e.g. three payments of $9.95 for a roughly $30 book, rely on the buyer hearing '$9.95', not '$30'.

Rich Schefren's Strategic Profits waits until month three to offer an upsell, because cancellation likelihood drops sharply after month three, and appends the upsell's payments to the end of the schedule rather than charging immediately.
caveats: The source advises running all promotional copy, especially time-limited offers, past an attorney; installment and trial terms have regulatory implications.
This relies on the buyer's tendency to discount future payments. It can attract buyers who later churn; measure total collected, not first-payment conversions.

cards.title: The magic of a dollar and the magic of a penny
cards.summary: 'Free' is powerful but a dollar-and-a-penny offer is nearly as powerful, because it changes the framing and sometimes enables a physical gimmick.
cards.use_when: Packaging a paid offer so it can be advertised at a near-zero entry price, or splitting a price so a component can honestly be advertised at $1.
steps: Consider whether part of the offer can be split so a component is advertised at one dollar or one penny while the essential component carries the real price.

Example: an integrated accounting suite at $249 was split into modules at $1 each plus a $244 general ledger that every module required. The 'accounting software for a dollar' mailing generated 10 times more orders than the 'integrated accounting software for $249' control.

A commercial cleaning company was advised to charge one penny instead of cleaning for free, so it could spot-glue a penny to the top of the sales letter: 'We will clean your offices or plant for only a penny … and we've even enclosed the penny to get you started!'
caveats: The source describes this as a gimmick that worked; the 10x result is one company's control comparison.
The penny/spot-glue tactic is direct mail specific. The transferable idea for ecommerce is splitting a price so a component can honestly be advertised at $1.

cards.title: Drop-in-the-bucket technique to preempt sticker shock
cards.summary: Build the perception of value and compare the price to larger alternatives before stating it, so the actual figure lands as a drop in the bucket.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page or sales page for a product priced above the obvious reference category, including e-books and information products.
steps: Explain what the product actually is and where its value comes from before revealing price; reframe it away from the cheap comparison category.
Compare the price to the cost of hiring the author or expert. The source's example: a $79 e-book compared to 'well over $25,000' of accumulated work and 'about $200 an hour' for a lawyer.
Stack descending numbers so the final price feels small: 'won't cost you $25,000 … or $1,000 … or even $200. Instead, the price is just $79.'
Add delivery and access benefits in the same breath (immediate download, no shipping, no waiting).

Mike Pavlish's framing: convince the prospect the price is a drop in the bucket compared to the value received, and do it before you give the price. The source says it uses this for every offer, not just high-priced ones.
caveats: Values cited in the copy must be traceable to something real (the author's rates, the price of alternatives), or the anchor collapses under scrutiny.
For ecommerce, translate the anchor into real substitute costs: assembly, installation, professional service, or replacing the item later.

cards.title: Twelve ways to overcome sticker shock
cards.summary: A checklist of tactics beyond drop-in-the-bucket for making a high price acceptable.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a high-priced product page or offer where the price is revealed and resistance is expected.
steps: 1. Compare the product's cost to the cost of hiring the author (the source cites $500/hour, so an e-book costs 'less than five minutes of my time').
2. Make the prospect relieved to hear your price by stating higher prices for other options first (laser eye surgery $1,000, optician glasses $300, your specs $19.95).
3. Make apples-to-oranges comparisons against other information resources, not direct competitors (a $297 subscription vs. $5,000 for one speech from a top speechwriter).
4. Spread out payments; 'till forbid' monthly credit card billing is one form.
5. State the price in the smallest true terms, e.g. per day.
6. Value the component parts and show their retail sum exceeds the bundle price.
7. Add an element the buyer cannot easily price, like a CD-ROM with a loose-leaf service, to break direct comparison.
8. Use a calculator to dramatize compounding outcomes.
9. Pre-empt the objection by stating the high price up front and using it to exclude non-prospects.
10. Use a false close: bring the prospect to the point of ordering, then add another benefit before asking for the order.
11. Add a sweetener: extra premium, extended guarantee, free support, or two-for-one.
12. Establish yourself as the leading expert in your niche; price resistance diminishes with perceived authority.
caveats: Several of these tactics are framing devices; the underlying price and value must still be real to avoid refunds and reputation damage.

The compounding-math example ('5 percent monthly for 10 years turns $10,000 into $3.4 million') is an illustrative dramatization, not a forecast. Do not present hypothetical returns as likely outcomes.

cards.title: Good-better-best pricing to raise average order value
cards.summary: Offer three tiers and expect the middle to win, while the low and free tiers defuse 'too expensive' objections and feed a funnel.
cards.use_when: Structuring product tiers, bundles or supplement-style multi-packs on a product page or pricing page.
steps: Build a ladder from free content, to a $10–50 book/e-book, to a $100–300 self-study package, to mid-range coaching with some personal contact, to high-touch premium consulting priced in the thousands.

For physical products, the equivalent three options are: a large supply at a discount with free premiums and free shipping (best value), a mid-size supply with one bonus and free shipping, and a single unit with no premiums and paid shipping.
Expect the majority to take the middle option; the cheapest feels insufficient and the most expensive feels excessive.
The presence of the low-priced and free options makes it hard for prospects to accuse you of being overpriced, since you can point them to the cheaper ways to access your knowledge.
Use the ladder as a sales funnel to move buyers up to higher packages over time.
caveats: The source states the middle-option preference as a rule that holds with almost every product, but gives no measured conversion split.
Tier design must keep the middle option genuinely adequate; a deliberately crippled middle tier damages trust.

cards.title: The four guarantee decisions: length, conditionality, coverage, activation
cards.summary: A guarantee has four design levers, and longer plus unconditional generally lifts response while conditions and ambiguity suppress it.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising a guarantee for a product page, especially high-priced or downloadable products.
steps: Length: the minimum used in direct marketing is 10 days; a two-week guarantee is common for trading services so the window closes before buyer's remorse; 30 days is the most common; the source prefers 60 or 90 days. Lifetime guarantees are not recommended for solo entrepreneurs because they leave a permanent liability, and dated information products shouldn't carry long guarantees.

Conditionality: avoid conditional guarantees such as 'in saleable condition' or 'show a sincere effort'. Buyers fear the seller will claim they used the materials wrong and refuse the refund. The unconditional guarantee works best and should be stated as such: 'no questions asked.'

Coverage: decide whether shipping and handling is refunded. If it is not, say 'product refund' rather than 'full refund'. The source does not refund shipping and handling; some sellers go further and pay return shipping.
Activation: the clock should run from receipt of goods, not order date, and the copy should spell out exactly how to get a refund (e.g. return the unused portion, or even the empty bottles).
caveats: Double-your-money-back guarantees can be powerful; the source cites a doctors' oral board workshop where adding it tripled attendance and revenue. That is an example, not a benchmark.
The source is explicit that it is not giving legal advice; consult an attorney on guarantee terms and any persistent-customer disputes.
Directories and time-sensitive digital products should not get long guarantees, because a buyer could use the edition for a year and then return it.

cards.title: Make the guarantee visually prominent
cards.summary: A guarantee buried in small print does not do its job; set it in larger type inside a bordered or certificate-style block.
cards.use_when: Laying out a product page, sales page or email that contains a guarantee.
steps: Give the guarantee its own headline in large bold type.
Set the guarantee body copy around 12-point type.
Put a box or certificate-style border around the guarantee block.
Do not hide the guarantee in body copy or an asterisked footnote in 8-point type.

Write the terms clearly to avoid misinterpretation. Example rewrite from the source: instead of a performance-only condition, say 'If you do not make extra money trading options with our program, or you are not 100 percent satisfied for any other reason — or for no reason — just return the program within 90 days for a full refund.'
caveats: Prominence only helps if the terms are simple; a visually bold but conditional guarantee still raises suspicion.

cards.title: Unfair advantage offer for digital products
cards.summary: For downloadable products the buyer cannot return, let them keep the file with a refund, trading a small amount of abuse for a large lift in conversion.
cards.use_when: Selling e-books, PDF courses, templates or other non-returnable digital downloads where refunds usually mean the buyer keeps the file anyway.
steps: State the guarantee so the buyer keeps the product after a refund: 'I'll send you a prompt refund … and you can still keep the e-book with my compliments.'
Actively surface the buyer's ability to take advantage, e.g. that they may use a software tool during the 30-day window, recode their systems, and still return it.
The source's e-book refund rate is described as a tiny fraction of 1 percent, and conversion rose after adding the copy.
David Powers tested telling buyers they could keep the e-book either way and reported a 21 percent increase in conversion and sales.
For the Y2K software case cited, explicitly offering the use-then-return path was very profitable and returns were no higher than normal.
caveats: The 21 percent figure is one marketer's test result, not a promise.
Requiring deletion of a downloaded file is unenforceable, so the source does not require it.
Works because most buyers are honest; monitor actual refund rates before rolling out broadly.

cards.title: Use deadlines to force an act-now decision
cards.summary: Time limits are the simplest urgency mechanism; choose a specific date only if you control timing, otherwise use a generic response window.
cards.use_when: Adding urgency to a promotion, email, landing page or checkout banner.
steps: Pick one of two formats: a specific date ('Offer expires March 15, 2009') or a generic window ('You must reply within 15 days').

Use a specific date only if printing, emailing or page timing is under control, so the piece does not arrive after the date. If you print in large quantities or mail continuously, use the generic window so it works whenever the piece lands.

Set length by channel: for direct mail, 15–21 days is reasonable. For email, shorter windows work ('this week only', 'expires in 48 hours'), and one or two follow-up reminder emails near the deadline generate additional orders.
On a landing page, display a real-time clock or counter of days or hours remaining.
For consumer direct mail, a 7-, 11- or 15-day reply window with a quick-response bonus (a free report for replying within seven days) is common.
Infomercials compress this further: eliminate one installment for callers within 20–30 minutes, equivalent to a 25 percent discount.
caveats: The source explicitly advises running promotional copy past an attorney, especially time-limited offers: once you state an expiry date, you generally cannot extend it.
A deadline that is not enforced trains the audience to ignore future deadlines.

cards.title: Trial length: test 30 vs. 60 vs. 90 days and the word 'trial' vs. 'use'
cards.summary: A longer trial can lift response until it hits a ceiling, and replacing 'trial' with 'use' can lift it further when the word 'trial' carries negative work connotations.
cards.use_when: Designing free-trial or free-use offers for software, subscriptions or products that require setup/learning effort.
steps: Test trial length against your standard. In the source's mainframe software case, 60 days outperformed the standard 30 days by 10 percent; 90 days produced no further lift over 60.

Diagnose why the standard length fails. The source's conclusion: 30 days was not enough for a busy IT professional to install and test software, so prospects returned it feeling the window was expiring before they had tested it.

Then test the label. In the same company's mailing, '60-day free use' outperformed '60-day free trial' by 15 percent, because 'trial' connoted broken batch files and weekend testing, while 'use' felt positive.

Apply the same logic to ecommerce SaaS and subscription offers: give enough time for the product to be actually used before the billing decision, and name the offer after the benefit rather than the risk.
caveats: Both results are single-company split tests; the direction is a hypothesis for your audience.
Longer trials delay cash collection and increase the window for cancellation.

cards.title: Limit quantity or enrollment with a credible reason
cards.summary: Scarcity via limited quantity, limited seats or limited membership works best when the limitation is specific, credible and true.
cards.use_when: Promoting product launches, drops, limited-edition runs, cohort courses or capacity-constrained services where supply is genuinely finite.
steps: Use the limited-number framing: 'This offer is limited to the first 200 people who respond.' The source notes this works because recipients don't know how many were mailed.

Give a legitimate reason for the limit. Examples: prototyping capacity constrained by staff ('If you are not one of the first to respond, you may well have to wait longer than we'd both like'); a $1,500 advisory service capped at 1,000 subscribers because the publisher could not otherwise ensure good trade execution, with copy stating checks would be returned uncashed past the cap.
For events, seminars and workshops, state that limited seats are first-come, first-served.
A scarcity line can be literally true and still convey limited supply, e.g. Bill Jayme's 'Only so many copies of the premiere issue will be printed — no more.'
Use early-bird discounts for events and pre-publication offers: a $500 discount on a $2,497 seminar; even $5–10 off a $100 book or directory can lift response.
caveats: The source warns not to sacrifice credibility. A 'we printed only 1,000 copies' claim fails when the premium is a downloadable PDF or MP3, since the company could obviously print more.
Invented limits can work, but the source advises respecting the prospect's intelligence; a transparently fake cap destroys the tactic.

cards.title: Choose premiums differently for lead generation than for sales
cards.summary: For sales, premium desirability matters most (Benson); for lead generation the source favors premiums related to the product to avoid unqualified freebie seekers.
cards.use_when: Selecting a premium for a purchase offer versus a lead magnet for opt-ins or B2B inquiries.
steps: Per Dick Benson, the primary criteria for premium selection are perceived value and desirability; relevance to the product is secondary. Benson's view is that a premium need not relate to the product.

The source partly disagrees: in lead generation, a desirable premium matters, but the source puts more weight on a premium related to the product, because unrelated high-value premiums bring in freebie seekers and unqualified leads.

For B2B and corporate buyers, be aware that some organizations forbid employees from accepting vendor gifts (defense contractors are cited). A mail test of a 25 percent discount versus the same discount plus a free clock radio found the premium depressed response. Possible reason given: buyers feared being seen as accepting a bribe, or assumed the price included the gift's cost.

If you offer a B2B premium, consider making it relevant to the buyer's company rather than personal, so the buyer looks like a sharp purchaser. The cited example: a free CD-ROM stacker/reader offered with a group of high-priced CD-ROM information products.
caveats: The depressed-response test is described as business-gift-specific; do not generalize it to consumer ecommerce without testing.
The source presents the Benson disagreement explicitly, so this is a situational choice, not a single rule.
